blocks.x: Okay, you want to say a few words?
Mm-hmm.
Go ahead and talk anything you want to.
Well, let's see what I've got to say for you.
Okay, it's all.
This is Lynn Joe Nicholas.
When were you born?
I forgot the date of that.
Once you told me the date is 2nd or 22nd?
22nd.
22nd. Where were you born?
My freshman and my father.
Did any of your folks play music?
Well, my brother used to play in Orange County. He used to go around. He used to go around. He used to play good. Get the date. Kind of.
Did you have any?
I was daddy.
Did you have many brothers and sisters?
I had two brothers and two sisters.
Which one was the Albert Nicholas was then your neck for you, wasn't he?
One of them.
One of your brothers. Brother or sister? Brother. That's right. He'd be your brother Charles, his name was Nicholas. What instrument did you take up first?

Mm-hmm . I guess I put all the rest down. Well I could play them. I never forget them. I could play them. And that's why I got a carnet. I didn't know. I was playing climbing that's good. Playing with Joe Alvarez. I was playing with Joe Alvarez. I was playing with Joe Alvarez. I was watching him while he was playing with Joe Alvarez. He was kind of lazy. He didn't like to play too much. He said, I dropped him. Joe dropped him. I said, well, I said, just four pieces, just three. Then I said, well, I don't know. I said, all of them, I'm going to drop those strips. And he went out. And the guy's gun gets up. He went around about 25, 20, 25. It stayed a long time. I played about, I played one tune first and the people come around there and I never see. He starts with him. Who was with me? I played. I played about five, six numbers. And first thing, and after I said, oh, I played all the way. And didn't have no horn. Didn't play. He didn't have nothing. That was the second time I tried. I tried a carnet. And after that, I got off. There was a little brass. I loaned to Bunk. Bunk, I took a listen. I took a listen with him. I loaned to him. I used to leave him, so I didn't take a straight away when I played. And so I took it back. I went to playing, playing, playing. First thing you know, I put the clandest down. Played the corner. And first I went to play with the bass player. That's the manager of the band.
Who else was in the band when Oliver was there at Abedee's? Who else? Do you remember? Was it Richard M Jones?
Oh yeah. Miney, Miney's name was, we used to call him Miney. Miney Jones. Joseph Jones.
Why did they call him Miney? I never knew.
I don't know. We used to call him Miney all the time.
Somebody said once, you know, when I knew him in Chicago, he used to limp a little bit. Yeah, yeah. Did he always limp too? Yeah.
Maybe there's something about his knee then, you think? Or was that... I don't know. It wasn't about that. There was something else he used to call me.
I never did know why. Somebody told me it was because of his knee that he limp. I didn't know. I didn't think it would be that, but I wondered.
Him and Tiff went together then, did they?
Who was the drummer? Do you remember?
Ernest Rogers.

Oh, Ernest Rogers. You know, he died, didn't you? Yes. In the short time. Yes. In September. I wanted to go to see him. I didn't know he did till the way after. I went to the funeral, but I didn't see him before. I'm sorry I didn't. Big strong looking, help the fella. Yeah.

Ernest Rogers did. That whole band is gone. What used to play there on Ronald Cronin. Ernest Rogers. I don't see how it's done. I don't get nothing about him anymore. The last Cronin that was playing there. I believe Charlie loved playing Cronin tonight.
Oh, yes. Charlie was playing there. He had his teeth pulled out this spring too, but I think he had his teeth this time.
Oh, yes. Oh, yes. Pete was playing there. Peter Boccage. He must have put it, given up, you know.
Go ahead, you were talking about Bunk when you went to Bunk to take lessons?

Yeah, I went to Bunk to take lessons. I took about ten lessons. And after that, every time I'd go by, I was trying to catch him. You'd never see that. Where did Bunk live in those days? Oh, on Villarreal Street.
Villarreal, about where on Villarreal Street?

There was between, I'd say between Tudor, between Fenton and the outcoaster. Yeah. On that side of the bank. Bunk would never come home. That's how they call him Bunk. You see Fenton. The other batter on the old bill batter in the bar, they'd go on knockout, put the junk in the pool. He'd never come home right away.
I never did know why they called him Bunk.
Yeah, that's why he was calling him Bunk. You have a bottle, you never bother the pool or nobody. You have a bottle wrapped up. You have something in it. Corp, little bottle, big bottle.
Big corp bottle.

One time I went to Bomber, say two weeks. They came there and asked me, he finished a band of band. He came there and asked me, was it a big fine person? Oh Joe, I didn't think of about three or four years. He said, uh huh Joe, how are you? You playing? I said, you playing again? He said, yeah, I'm almost gone. I said, well I'll be gone. I can't believe it. He said, I'm tired. He said, it's a little good but I can't play much anymore.
He lost his teeth then. He gave up his money.
Yeah, he had no teeth. He had no teeth then. He gave up his money. Well, he had small teeth that looked good. That looked just like a plate.
He played alright then.
But some, they ain't no good. You can't get used to everything so good. Like you would with your own teeth, you know?
Oh no, they wouldn't be as good as your own teeth.

No, you couldn't be. You never make it. You make it for nothing much as good as that. And he said, you want a drink? You have to take a bottle. I said, uh huh. He said, take a little. I said, I'll take a little. I used to drink but I didn't drink like they drink, you know? I took a drink. I took a drink. I took a drink. I said, whiskey. I said, you're going to play tonight? He said, we didn't even think so. We used to play, everybody else was going to play. I said, we didn't know that. People didn't tell us. They said, I don't take the truth. You know what's the matter? They didn't believe us. We never come up for something. We never show up. I've happened to that. He didn't know when we were going to play the truth. He said, well, I said, oh. And then they told him something like that. I don't know if we were going to play that. And so I said, well, I said, we do. We'll let y'all play. He said, no, no, no, no, you play, you play. I said, you the one next time. I'm going to get the world to play. I said, you the one to play. I said, what's the difference? I said, I don't want to see the place. I said, I said, you play, you play. I said, all right, we play. We play and we packed the house up. We jammed up. And he didn't play. Yeah, he played that next night. The Walhurst would play, but we wouldn't play. That was in Beaumont. Yeah, in Beaumont, Texas. And we played the night after. Let's see who was to come there. No, no, no. Tuxedo, man. That's right. Tuxedo.

Did you ever run into Lazy Daddy, a piano player over there? Lazy Daddy Fillmore, they called him. The Bunkers used to talk about him. Other people say he's dead now. Yeah. Did you hear him? Did you ever play with him?
No, I never played with him. I wasn't.
How was he? Pretty good?
Yeah, he was good. Good.
I wanted to go down in the recording, but before I could find Barry Rubs, I heard he was dead. Yeah. He'd been down in Corpus Christi for a while.
Mm-hmm. He had a good band. Bunker had a good band. He was the worst one in the band.
That was the banner band.
Yeah, he could play, but he wouldn't play after that. That's how he played about.
Well his teeth were gone, I guess, and he couldn't do so well maybe then.

Uh-uh. Eddie wasn't about the teeth that much. It wasn't that. Eddie never was no loud trumpet player, you know. He used to play soft and sweet. Low, you know. Yeah. All the way he had his own teeth. He used to clean up all of them for that.
He never, that's what I always heard too. He wasn't really powerful. No.

But he could play. Like Bolden or Keppard. No, but he could play, I'm telling you, I'm supposed to scale it. Marlon. I was talking with him. He said, you got to do watching, I drew. You coming out good. Watch, you watch your, the only one I'm telling you to watch, I watch it. I, I, I don't know. I said, you see that there's a bunk there? I said, yeah. Oh, I said, he can play, man. He can make some stuff, he said. But I said, you got to watch. You got to watch your, the only one I watch you. I, I scared nobody but him. I mean, he could play. He's a good finger, you know, he had good fingers.
So he had a beautiful tone.
Yes.
That's what Louie said.
What? Yeah, he had a tone, take you off your feet. You could make it.
So how did Oliver play when you were with him? Was he real powerful or?

Oh, what the powerful corners, him and Fred, his powerful corners, Fred, I had you. Really was. They said, I don't know if they looked like it. They had some in them. They loved it. But they was, all the time, you know, show up.
Did he use a lot of the mute, or did he ever use a plunger, or his hand, or how did he do all that freak stuff, as they call it?
Who, uh, Joe, Joe, Joe, Joe, didn't use anything on that. This one, the last I seen there was a picture, was a mute, but he didn't use no mute.
You used open-hearted down here most of the time.
Oh, he used to make all kinds of stuff. Fred, Fred didn't use nothing either.
Oh, Fred, no.
Fred could make himself. He could be Joe.
Was Kempern as powerful a horn?

Yeah, a horn. Yeah, a horn. It was powerful in Joe, I believe it was. Yeah, it was powerful. Yeah, it was powerful. And he never did play soft, like we would do, but it sounds, it's got a good tone, you know? And this guy could blow. See, see, the only one he fell is bunk. He told me that many times. He said, bunk, I said, he was right. The old bunk, we'd be up in the corner, we'd buy a stuff, and I'd be all set in my life, all time sleeping. He'd never go home, you know? That was rough. He'd drink all the time with a bottle. You never worry, you never actually no bottle or nothing. He had his own stuff. Him and Fred had the same thing. Fred had his own stuff. And he was naming him about the morning and all, like you know, he was full of home, but nobody was making for nothing.
Tell us about Bowling. Did you ever, you heard Bowling when you were a boy, I guess?

I used to play flute them times, I heard Bowling. That's how I learned how to play. I used to play clarinet thing. I used to get that out the hall, at the Gloves Hall, or either at the Column 8 or 9, he didn't play at the Column 8 much, or at the Gloves.
Did he play at the Perseverance Hall, I think somebody said too, maybe down there on the?
Durden Street.
Yeah, I don't know. How many?
Durden Street. Durden Street. He didn't play that much neither.
Where was the Globe Hall? That's right by the, you see where the auditorium was?
Right there. Is it still there, that building? No, it broke down. That's where they had to take it down to the building of the auditorium.
I wondered.
I thought maybe it was on St. Peter's. It was still there. It was big place, sure, yeah. It's torn down.
I wondered. And old Bowling used to blow them down there, I'm telling you.
That's the part of the strong farm, I think. All the way through. It never, never come here and come down. It's put it down there. It's all regained.
It's all regained.
It's all regained.
Who else was in this band? Do you remember when you heard him?
Oh, I remember all of them. I forget some of them names, but I know them.
There was a trombonist, Cornish. Was he with him then?
Oh yeah, that was all the band. That's what I kind of saw it out with. There was a trombonist and George, Louis, Louis. Frank Louis.
You mentioned you saw him once across the lake, you said just a few years ago.

Yeah, I see him. I thought he was dead or he quit playing something. He had a case. He knows me. He's like, now he called me first. He said, you think you're? I said, yeah. I said, where you going, Louis? He said, man, I come from playing back there. He said, where you going? I said, I'm going over there by the Tunk. He said, Tunk, what do you want to go play over there? I said, well, we can't see it all hot and cold out here. You go make up with it. We don't know. We play the solan. They might actually play. We play some. We make a couple of dollars, man. And it's warming up all the time. It keeps nice warming up. Which hall was that? At Mandeville?
Mandeville.
Yeah.
Is that right where they had a boat in those days, didn't they? Yeah.
A boat. A boat.
And when was it you played then? Mandeville. I mean, what kind of a hall was it? Right at the ferry place?
Yeah, yeah.
Right on the shore then?
Right. It was about four blocks on the center side. Not all up that floor, but two blocks or three blocks. That's where I met Bunk before he got playing here.
Is that right? I know Bunk was over there for a while.
Bunk used to stay over there.
Yeah. In Mandeville.
Yeah, he used to stay over there. I know he used to teach the band. A whole lot of, he learned a whole lot of fellas. Band. Yeah. He had a good band, too.

I know Tommy Ladner, he said, learned from him over there in the band. Yeah. Did you know Tommy Ladner? He left here when he was real young. I guess you didn't know him much. Went to Chicago and played a lot up there. Where did he play?
Trumpet.
Oh, kind of a light fella.
Yeah. Well, he was a light fella. Yeah, yeah. I know him. He was a light fella. He was a little old. I know him.
I see him play.
He was a small fella.
Yeah. He worked in Chicago a lot, then went to New York. But I guess he didn't play much here at all.

No. But Uncle Lonnie taught a lot of fellas around here. They had a good band on that lick there, too. You know what I'm saying? It looked like they didn't know nothing but sure he'd get to play in there. Cliff Bass, the drummer he did. He died not so long ago. That was a drummer. Look at that fella.
What was his name?
Cliff Bass. I forgot his last name. He's brother. He's got a brother, Frank Connick. That bright fella.
Can you remember any more about Bowden? Where did you hear him? Aside from Globe Hall, did you ever go out to Lincoln Park?

Lincoln Park. I went to all the park. Jonathan Park. He was all over. I used to like him. He was playing the most of the other corners. He was playing the most of the corners of the world. Nothing in the city. And every way he would play, he could have the best corner, the best corner player. Supposed to be. Yeah. When he played against some other fellas, he'd have the crowd. But when all the little house cover would get out there and start the showin' out, he'd never sit down. He'd stand up all the time.
He'd always sit up.

Where'd he go? It's just a man for us to be skint. It happened with that little boy. You know I used to, they were on La Perouse and Pril. And he was out the background. He could hear him just like I thought he was right there. Sometimes I didn't feel like going out. I'd sit down at the corner. He'd get old Bolden, show him out of every number. He'd kill them all. All of them. Man used to play for the strong too, because I don't like Bolden.
What pieces did Bolden play? Do you remember? Did he play a lot of blues or what? Oh, a whole lot of blues.
He played everything. Paddle on the slope. And the other blues. A whole lot of blues. That's what he used to play more.
And he played Careless Love, do you remember?

Yeah, yeah. He played all of them. I believe they say I could admit, but I believe he made that up. He played everything. Every piece was the side. Some of them was out there like you, but he played all that.
Do you remember in those days that anybody played Tiger Rag or that?
Yeah, yeah. He played that.
He played that too.

Yeah. Tiger Rag. Tiger Rag. Tiger Rag. Well, he used to call it Tiger Rag back then though. No, he used to call it something else, but he played that. He used to call it Tiger too, no one time I remember. The other number he used to play. And they could paddle behind the door, I'm a good man, won't never know, and all that. He could make all kinds of songs. And I never seen him with no music. I don't know if he really did watch, you know. I never seen him with nothing he could play some of that pieces. And he played what these fathers of the Reers could play and what they couldn't play.
How was his range? Did he play up high a good deal or down low? Did he hit a lot of high notes or low or how was, what kind of a song? Bust right on out.

Everything right on out. Up to the top. Never seen him, put his arm like a full thing, you know. I think Marty's tired, you know, he just keep up there too, look around, and he's a man to get ready to go out. The horn.
Did you ever use a mute or anything?

No, I never seen him with nothing like that. Just an open horn. The groove wall, it was upstairs. High. And I'd be on that side by the bottom, by the gym, looking at him. I'd love him just dancing, doing nothing, just standing up, bummer nobody, beat his arm, watch and listen, you know. I'd get off to myself. That joke was, Nick, he was decent. He'd have to put something in here. He looked at the horn and he had the other side of the back.
Like Artesian Hall still has that, you remember Artesian Hall, the balcony up over the door? Uh huh. It's one of those, like that, something like that.
Yeah, like that. All the halls like that, there's one. All the halls, huh?
I've never been inside Economy Hall. Economy Hall is like that.
The cooperators got two on each other. Well, the cooperators, that hall is still here, I believe somebody. Yeah, yeah, they got a church out there.
Oh, a church. I've never seen it. I'll have to find where that is.
Got some, uh, uh, spiritual church, you know. Which street?
Spiritual church. Oh, yes.
Which street is it on, though? Liberty Street. Liberty Street. Liberty Street.
Yeah, you can.
That's not the old Hopes Hall, is it?
That's not the same thing. Yeah.
Copperators, Copperators, Copperators, that's when it's called the Hopes.
Well, that's the Hopes Hall then, too.
Oh, I didn't know that. I know where that is.
Sure. That's the old name. Yeah, that's on Liberty.
That's the old name then cooperators. Oh, I didn't know. I wondered. I wondered. Yeah. So that's the, you've seen that, Hope Hall.
Yeah.
Yeah. Great big place, a great big church.

I used to play that all the time. Sure, I know it then. I wondered if I, how I missed it all. I played in every hall, every hall, I'd be more, more, picked more than anybody else. In, in, in, just playing, you know. I played in every hall.
I played in every hall. I played in every hall.
I played in every hall. I can't call them all.

I just played in the Calcariators, New Hall, police events, police events, the, the, the all, the, all the stuff, all the crap. Yeah. Yeah. I played, uh, bones on me, rickety, shens on me. Yeah. I have pictures of quite a few of those halls.
I used to take my camera around and get pictures of them. Most of the halls were downtown.
Yeah, most of them were downtown. Most of them were downtown. All of them were downtown. Yes.
There was a few up, the Longshoreman's Hall way uptown. Yeah, up there.

Well, I didn't play, I didn't play in that hall much. Didn't play that much? Much, I played, I didn't play much. There was another one called Old Providence Hall uptown on St. Dope. Well, I played in that, played in that.
Well, not St. Dope, on Dope.
I played in the Harlem Hall, every, uh, the, uh, oh, again.
The San Suu Kee was, uh, was that a hall built?
Yeah, that's a hall, that's a hall of San Suu Kee. It was a big one too.
It was on the Howard Avenue. That's quite a way of town.

Yeah. I'm just gonna see. The, uh, the Hall, that, uh, oh, it looked like all of them, all that church built on them. I don't have to take them down someday, which is good to find. Oh, they leave it and just take something off and they take.
Yeah, a lot of them are church.
Well, uh, they had, uh, that's why I used to see Bowling most of the time. Out on, on Padilla Street, he used to play there, the King's Hall. King's Hall. King's Hall. He used to. Oh yes, Kennies.
Okay. Then the Masonic Hall was up there too. Yeah. That's the one they used to call Funky Butt Hall, I think. Some people called it that.
That's the King's Hall, it's called Funky Butt. Yes.
That was a church, I guess that's torn down now.
Oh, no, it's that, but the bit that put the add-on to the mid is better, even the nicer. Yeah. The, I forgot the name of the church. That's the old hall.
I took a picture of that here, I have a picture of that on Perdido, that was right on Perdido.
Yeah.
Yep. Perdido, what was that? Yeah, that's pretty close to Liberty, right? Yeah.
Mm-hmm. Like between the bottom. That was, that's how I used to.
That was called Kennies? Kennies Hall.
Kennies. No, that's Kennies Hall.
Was that the name of a man that owned it or?

Well, he owned a couple of them halls. He owned that, Kennies Hall, Kegas Hall. He owned a couple of them, and he had a hardy, he had a hardy, he used to run it now. I don't know if he was hitting the wood. He used to have a good crowd, I think everything was packed. That's why before he was hit, he had a swell play clown that he did too, I believe in that. George. George. George Bocquet. George Cobwell.
Well, no George.
Who? Cobwell. Cobwell. Yeah, he's been that long.
That's right.
He used to be the clown that tall, brown-skinned fella.
Who were some of the other good clarinet players in those days that you used to watch and listen to?

Well, the son of a woman I used to watch, and he used to play so much all the time, left for the other folks I wouldn't be playing. He'd be sitting down, fooling around. That's George Lewis. George Lewis. Bert and Bakke and all of them.
Did you hear the TOs? How were they?

He used to do better than all of them, all of them. To me, I don't know about it but to me. He used to have to work, work with everybody. He used to blow a clarinet. I tried many times practically, but I never could do it. He'd never come out like that, ain't he? Puffy jawed out. He'd never go out like that. He'd never seen him look like he ain't blind.
Never did puff him out then?
No, I'd puff at all. He'd puff from the inside.
Yeah, didn't move his...
From the inside. He'd never go in like that. He'd never go out like that.
Was that Lorenzo TO?
No, George Lewis.
Oh, George Lewis or that Frank Lewis you mean?
Frank Lewis, yeah. Frank Lewis. Frank Lewis. Well, that's two Lewis. I didn't know George was playing back then. And then George Lewis played something like Frank Lewis.
Yeah.

And I used to judge him many times. I said, George, you used to go over at Lake Two. You used to show that when you was little now. I said, I believe George you're a poor boy. He said, I don't know. I said, you're a son. I said, well, that's going to make you ain't nothing in your daddy. I said, man, this is a half children and women and they're gone. You never see them anymore, you know? Yeah, that's right. I believe that's George's daddy too. Lil Frank Lewis was a sharp old guy. You really didn't think he might have been? I didn't think he might have been.
I didn't think he was George's father. Yeah, yeah.
I never did ask him about his father. He don't talk much about it. No, he don't talk about that. Nobody, nobody. No, never said a word about it. I asked him a couple of times.
And his mother, you know, is named Zeno now. Yeah.
I don't know if she was married again.
But he was married again. And then they're gone.
They're gone.
They're gone. They're gone.
They're gone. They're gone. They're gone. They're gone.
They're gone.
They're gone. They're gone.
I don't know if they were married again. I don't know if they were married or what. I ought to ask her sometime. I mean, I wonder if she was any relation to this.
It was a drummer, wasn't there, Zeno? Henry Zeno. I wonder if she was any relation to him.
They had a couple of Zenos around here. I usually call his mother Mrs. Lewis, but her real name is Mrs. Zeno, Alice Zeno. He might be a part.

There might be some relation. There might be some relation. There might be a part. I'm telling you. Jerry don't talk much, you know. Oh, did you ever hear Charlie McCurdy much? How was he on clarinet? Well, he was great. You know, he was playing nothing but strictly music, you know, and make all kinds of sweet – really harmonious stuff. He was good. Who did he play with? Do you know?
Oh, he played with all them bands.
All the bands. All the bands. All the bands. The last band they had to meet up, they had the Peerless band. Peerless, yeah.
Peerless, yeah.
That was with Bab Frank.
Oh, he played piccolo, didn't he?
Yeah, he left them, yeah. He never come back. That old boy's prison piccolo though. Bab Frank.
What kind of a part did they play in the band? You played piccolo too, you said.
Yeah, playing things like a clarinet. Just like clarinet.
It's like clarinet.
Yeah, I think it would be good in the band.
They play a piccolo inside with the band or is that strictly for a parade in the way? Inside of the band.

Inside of the band. For dancing? Dancing. Inside of the band. I mean, I've made a piccolo player, you know. Players, I mean, like that. That's Frank and all that kind of. That's the only one I know, that's Frank. I knew he could make that thing talk. And he played just quite a bit like a clarinet. Played like a clarinet, played a clarinet, all those different things. You had a rascal man who'd look like he wouldn't be playing but he's playing. Well, that's really sounding like something. It's good all right.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Did you ever play much in brass bands on the street? I know I used to hear you a few years ago. Yeah. Oh, Kid Thomas was telling us. He used to play with you. Yeah.
I played in all of them brass bands and played many, many, many, many, many. Three years ago.
Yeah. I played in all the brass land and played many, many, many, many, many, many, many rain down this morning, said nothing. Many pervades, and a rain down.
I ran down all the trombone players, actually, to the stage. I called them all, I called all about four or fifty.
Who are the names of them?

Yeah, they're dead. Just a few around. Yeah, I remember. I mean, what are their names? Oh, some of them I forgot their names. Ambrose. Ambrose Powers. George Washington. I called them Booger Man. I love them. Black, black, black. We used to call them Booger Man. And he was from over there. I asked him to go over there.
I don't know if he got the name or no. You're Frankie Dukes and I guess you played with him. I played with him once.

Once? I didn't want to play with him. He's crooked. He's funny. Really? Funny father. He's big and he played at times. I asked teacher, I was small, you know, just, when I was old. He said, I'm sitting in the house with George Washington. I was lying. He lied there. I said, well, I'll tell you what I want to play. Someone fired up. He said, well, that's what I want to get here. I said, oh, you didn't tell me that. I said, nothing. I said, I said, I know what you're saying, you know. I said, I'm going to fight out. I don't care what you're doing. It's the rest of them. They put them up the building and they're taking them. And he said, you know, you're on mute. I said, yeah, I said, I'm on mute. I know what you're saying to me. I said, I'm on mute. I'm on mute. So, he told me I'm like that. I went out there. Went to play him. Played. That's what he told me. After that, he was all. He looked at all. He looked at all. He looked at all.
He looked at all. He looked at all.

He looked at all. I said, Pike. And he said, that George Jones and a whole lot of the other folks coming up South I thought he was standing looking. I said, that's the best band. Two bands, you know? That's two bands. Yeah, you see, that's the best band. He said, Frank, why'd you get that band? You can scrape it from the club. He said, I got it.
